query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys outside the well-studied Nb-Ta and titanium-rich systems is governed by the combination of valence electron count (VEC) and localized pockets of nonrandom distributions, also called 'clustered ordering', which can be engineered through systematic experimentation and first-principles simulation.

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic experimentation and first-principles simulation to vary VEC and introduce clustered ordering in high-entropy alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of clustered ordering and increase in VEC do not enhance the superconducting properties, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Mechanical properties of single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs) can be unusually enhanced than many conventional single-phase engineering alloys (). Recent computational and experimental studies indicate that the atomic distribution in such solid solution HEAs may not be completely random as originally believed, but exhibit localized pockets of nonrandom distributions, also called “clustered ordering” (). While strengthening due to such local chemical clusters has been reported in Al (), Ni (), Fe () base alloys, and more recently, in complex bulk metallic glasses () and HEAs (, ), the ability to systematically engineer its nature and extent has so far eluded us. While the quinary CoCrFeNiMn, arguably the most extensively studied HEA, has been established as a single-phase alloy (), local chemical ordering was recently experimentally shown, and computationally validated, in its “subset” ternary CoCrNi alloy (, ) Similarly, direct experimental evidence of nonrandom atomic distributions has been presented in CoCrFeNiPd () and CoNiV () HEAs. In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. Through the proposed methodology, involving high-energy mechanical milling combined with sintering without the application of pressure, it was possible to manufacture high entropy alloys of the CuCrFeNiTiAlx system. Here, the effect of Al on the microstructure, phase evolution, and chemical behavior of the resulting alloys was studied. The following are the main conclusions reached in this study: The powder metallurgy process was proven as an effective experimental route to retain the characteristic microstructure of high entropy alloys. Since milling induces a finer particle size and high lattice distortion, both conditions facilitate metal bonding in the solid state. Furthermore, sintering promotes metal diffusion and, consequently, their solubility and sample densification. Based on the XRD studies, as the Al concentration increases, high entropy alloys undergo a microstructural transformation, from a single FCC phase to a mixture of coexisting phases made of FCC and BCC phases, as well as the precipitation of different compounds such as FeNi, Al3Ni, CrNiFe, TiAl, and Ti3Al.
